::: {#thm-partition-equivalence}
#### A partition gives an equivalence relation

Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a partition of a set $S$ (@def-set-partition),
and on $S$ let $a \sim b$ when $a$ and $b$ are in the same set in $\mathcal{C}$.
Then $\sim$ is an equivalence relation (@def-equivalence-relation),
and its equivalence classes (@def-equivalence-class) are exactly the sets in $\mathcal{C}$.

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

{{< slidebreak >}}

::: proof

**Reflexive.**
Each $a \in S$ is in some set in $\mathcal{C}$, so $a$ and $a$ are in the same set, and $a \sim a$.

**Symmetric.**
If $a$ and $b$ are in the same set in $\mathcal{C}$, then so are $b$ and $a$.

**Transitive.**
Suppose $a \sim b$ and $b \sim c$:
$a$ and $b$ are in a set $X \in \mathcal{C}$, and $b$ and $c$ are in a set $Y \in \mathcal{C}$.
Then $b \in X \cap Y$.
Different sets in $\mathcal{C}$ are disjoint, so $X = Y$,
and $a$ and $c$ are both in $X$, so $a \sim c$.

**Each class is a set in $\mathcal{C}$.**
Let $a \in S$, and let $X$ be the set in $\mathcal{C}$ that holds $a$.
An element $b$ has $b \sim a$ exactly when $b$ is in the set that holds $a$, which is $X$.
So $[a] = X$.

**Each set in $\mathcal{C}$ is a class.**
Let $X \in \mathcal{C}$.
Since $X$ is nonempty, it holds some element $a$,
and then $X = [a]$, by the previous step.

:::

:::
